q: Why does APBS 3.4.1's default geoflow-auto input syntax lack sufficient documentation in the paper's Appendix to run without access to the source-tree examples/geoflow/ directory?
basis: Our attempt to invoke the geometric-flow solver — a headline new capability of this paper — failed at input parsing with the Appendix-listed parameters (press, gamma, bconc, tolerance, etol, grid, vdwdisp). APBS reported syntax rejection at parse time. This creates a reproducibility gap: a reader in 2026 cannot exercise geoflow from the paper alone.
next_steps: Diff APBS-3.4.1 examples/geoflow/ against the paper's Appendix; identify keywords that are required but not documented; open a GitHub issue on Electrostatics/apbs to include a minimal working geoflow input file in the paper's supplementary material or an updated Appendix.

q: How closely do the PB-AM (analytical, coarse-grained sphere) and mg-auto (multigrid, atomistic) total solvation energies agree on a shared test protein, and at what sphere-cluster granularity does PB-AM's error become acceptable?
basis: PB-AM is claimed as a fast alternative for coarse-grained representations, but the paper does not publish head-to-head energy agreement with mg-auto on the same molecule. Our replication ran only mg-auto (1.096e5 kJ/mol on 1FAS), so we have no anchor for judging when PB-AM's coarse-graining is safe.
next_steps: Compute Δsolv(mg-auto) − Δsolv(PB-AM) for a spherical-ish small target (hexasaccharide, small α-helix bundle, or the barnase-barstar pair the paper features in Fig 3) as a function of sphere-cluster granularity, and fit an error model.

q: How sensitive is the LPBE→NPBE crossover salt concentration for weakly-to-moderately charged proteins?
basis: We observed <0.02% LPBE↔NPBE relative energy difference for 1FAS (net +4e) at 0.15 M NaCl, suggesting linearization is safe here. The paper does not quantify where nonlinear corrections become important. Practitioners default to LPBE for speed without a clear rule for when to escalate.
next_steps: Sweep salt concentration (0.01–1 M) and net charge (±1, ±5, ±20, ±100) on model systems and plot |E(NPBE) − E(LPBE)| / E(LPBE) contours. Publish a 'safe-to-linearize' region as guidance in the APBS docs.

q: What is the DX-file storage-cost vs numerical-precision tradeoff for large biomolecular systems, and would a lossy or binary alternative preserve visualization quality?
basis: Our 1FAS potential grid (1.6M points) produced a 21 MB ASCII DX file at default float64. Scaling to membrane-embedded protein complexes at similar resolution yields 1–10 GB files. The paper emphasizes the 3Dmol.js visualization workflow but does not discuss disk-footprint alternatives.
next_steps: Benchmark write-time, disk footprint, and downstream visualization/isosurface accuracy across DX ASCII vs OpenDX binary vs HDF5 vs lossy float16/bfloat16 grids. Assess whether 3Dmol.js could ingest a compressed format directly.

q: What is the practical parallel scaling of mg-para on modern (2024-era) NUMA hardware, and does the multigrid convergence rate hold on protein-complex systems 10–100× larger than the paper's canonical microtubule/ribosome demos?
basis: The paper cites mg-para as the parallel companion to mg-auto but our replication used single-CPU only. Modern node architectures (Sapphire Rapids, EPYC 9004, ARM Grace) have very different memory-bandwidth/core ratios vs the pre-2017 hardware on which the original multigrid convergence was measured. Convergence robustness at large problem size is a claim (C3, 'robust and scalable') we could not test.
next_steps: Run mg-para on progressively larger systems (1FAS → ribosome 4V5G → SARS-CoV-2 spike 6VXX) at 1, 4, 16, 64, 256 processes on a modern NUMA node; measure strong- and weak-scaling and report speedup vs mg-auto plus multigrid V-cycle count as a function of system size.
